\title{H-type foliation}

\section{H-type foliation}


H-type foliations were introduced by Baudoin, Grong, Rizzi and Vega-Molino as a geometric framework extending several important classes of sub-Riemannian structures, including H-type groups, \(K\)-contact manifolds and \(3K\)-contact manifolds; see \cite{Bau2022Htype}.
 
Let
\((M,\mathcal H,g)\) be a totally geodesic Riemannian foliation with orthogonal splitting
\[
    TM=\mathcal H\oplus\mathcal V,
\]
and let \(\nabla\) be the associated Bott connection with torsion \(T\). For
\(Z\in\mathcal V\), define \(J_Z:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) by
\[
    \langle J_ZX,Y\rangle
    =
    \langle Z,T(X,Y)\rangle,
    \qquad X,Y\in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal H}.
\]
The foliation is said to be of \textbf{H-type}(or Heisenberg-type) if
\[
    \langle J_ZX,J_ZY\rangle
    =
    |Z|^2\langle X,Y\rangle,
\]
or equivalently(by the skew-symmetry of $J_Z$),
\[
    J_Z^2=-|Z|^2\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal H}.
\]
Thus each vertical direction induces, after normalization, an orthogonal complex structure on the horizontal bundle. In particular, the horizontal distribution is bracket generating of step two, and the maps \(J_Z\) encode quantitatively the non-integrability of \(\mathcal H\).


\begin{definition}[\cite{Bau2022Htype}]
An H-type foliation is said to be 
\begin{itemize}
   \item  of \textbf{Yang-Mills type}, if $\delta _{\mathcal{H}}^{\nabla }T=0$;
   \item with horizontally parallel torsion, if $\nabla _{\mathcal{H}}T=0$;
   \item   with completely parallel torsion, if $\nabla T=0$.  
\end{itemize}	
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
	The Yang-Mills assumption plays an important role in the theory of generalized curvature dimension inequalities. 
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}
	On an H-type foliation, one has for every $X \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}}, Z \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{V}}$, 
	$$ -\pi _{\mathcal{V}}([X,J_Z X])=|X|^2Z. $$
	Thus, the horizontal distribution is bracket generating of step-two.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
	Note that 
	$$ -\pi _{\mathcal{V}}([X,J_Z X])=T(X, J_Z X) .$$
	By polarization, the H-type condition implies the Clifford relation
\begin{equation}\label{clif}
	J_ZJ_W+J_WJ_Z=-2\langle Z,W\rangle\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal H}.
\end{equation}
From this we see 
$$ \la -\pi _{\mathcal{V}}([X,J_{e_{\alpha }} X]), e_{\beta } \ra =- \la X,J_{e_{\beta }}J_{e_{\alpha }}X  \ra= \la X,J_{e_{\alpha }}J_{e_{\beta }}X  \ra+2 \delta _{\alpha \beta }|X|^2.$$
But 
$$ \la X,J_{e_{\alpha }}J_{e_{\beta }}X  \ra=- \la J_{e_{\alpha  }}X,J_{e_{\beta  }}X  \ra=  \la X,J_{e_{\beta }}J_{e_{\alpha }}X  \ra,$$
hence 
$$ \la -\pi _{\mathcal{V}}([X,J_{e_{\alpha }} X]), e_{\beta } \ra = \delta _{\alpha \beta }|X|^2.$$
\end{proof}

In fact, the proof states a slightly stronger pointwise fact: once you fix any nonzero horizontal vector \(X_p\),
\[
T_pM
=
\mathcal H_p+[X,\mathcal H]_p.
\]

\begin{theorem}[\cite{Bau2022Htype}]
	H-type foliations are Yang-Mills.
\end{theorem}

\section{Clifford representation}
The H-type condition endows the horizontal bundle with a natural
Clifford-module structure. Indeed,
we have seen from \eqref{clif} 
the following Clifford relation
\[
    J_ZJ_W+J_WJ_Z
    =
    -2\langle Z,W\rangle
    \operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal H},
    \qquad Z,W\in\mathcal V.
\]
Consequently, at each \(p\in M\), the map
\[
    \mathcal V_p\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_p),
    \qquad
    Z\longmapsto J_Z,
\]
extends naturally to a representation
\[
    J:\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal V_p)
    \longrightarrow
    \operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_p)
\]
of the Clifford algebra of \(\mathcal V_p\). In particular,
\[
    J_1=\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal H_p},
    \qquad
    J_{Z\cdot W}=J_ZJ_W,
\]
where \(Z\cdot W\) denotes Clifford multiplication. Thus compositions
of the operators \(J_Z\) are themselves encoded by the Clifford
algebra of the vertical space.

This representation provides a useful description of the algebra
generated by the vertical directions. Let \(\mathfrak a(p)\) denote
the Lie algebra of endomorphisms of \(\mathcal H_p\) generated by
\(\{J_Z:Z\in\mathcal V_p\}\), where the bracket is the commutator
\([A,B]=AB-BA\). As shown in
\cite{Bau2022Htype}, no higher-order commutators
are needed to generate \(\mathfrak a(p)\): it is generated by the
operators
\[
    J_Z
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    [J_Z,J_W].
\]
More precisely, either \(\{J_Z:Z\in\mathcal V_p\}\) is already closed
under commutators, or
\[
    \mathfrak a(p)
    \simeq
    \mathfrak{so}(k+1),
\]
where \(k=\dim\mathcal V\).

The first possibility is particularly restrictive. If the family
\(\{J_Z\}\) is itself closed under commutators, then either \(k=1\),
in which case the resulting structure is of complex type, or \(k=3\),
in which case the operators \(J_Z\), together with the identity,
satisfy the quaternionic multiplication rules. In the latter case one
can choose a local orthonormal vertical frame
\(\{Z_1,Z_2,Z_3\}\) such that, up to orientation,
\[
    J_{Z_1}J_{Z_2}=J_{Z_3},\qquad
    J_{Z_2}J_{Z_3}=J_{Z_1},\qquad
    J_{Z_3}J_{Z_1}=J_{Z_2},
\]
and
\[
    J_{Z_\alpha}^2=-\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal H}.
\]
This motivates the notion of an H-type foliation of
\emph{quaternionic type}; in particular, such a foliation necessarily
has vertical rank three. Important examples include \(3K\)-contact,
\(3\)-Sasakian, and quaternionic Heisenberg geometries.

If, in addition, the torsion is horizontally parallel,
\[
    \nabla_{\mathcal H}T=0,
\]
then the above algebraic type is independent of the point. Indeed,
parallel transport along horizontal curves intertwines the operators
\(J_Z\), while the H-type condition implies that \(\mathcal H\) is
bracket generating. Hence the Clifford-algebra structure at one point
determines the corresponding structure throughout the connected
manifold.

\section{H-type groups}

H-type foliations may be viewed as a geometric generalization of the classical H-type groups introduced by Kaplan (cf. \cite{Kapl1980Htype} or \cite{Bau2022Htype}). 

Recall that an H-type group is a connected simply connected two-step nilpotent Lie group \(G\) whose Lie algebra admits an orthogonal decomposition
\[
    \mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak z,
\]
where \(\mathfrak z\) is the center of \(\mathfrak g\), such that
\[
    [\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h]\subset\mathfrak z,
    \qquad
    [\mathfrak g,\mathfrak z]=0.
\]
For \(Z\in\mathfrak z\), define \(J_Z:\mathfrak h\to\mathfrak h\) by
\[
    \langle J_ZX,Y\rangle
    =
    \langle Z,[X,Y]\rangle .
\]
The H-type condition is
\[
    J_Z^2=-|Z|^2\operatorname{Id}_{\mathfrak h},
    \qquad Z\in\mathfrak z.
\]
The left translations of \(\mathfrak h\) and \(\mathfrak z\) determine, respectively, the horizontal and vertical distributions \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal V\), and the cosets of the center form the leaves of a totally geodesic Riemannian foliation. In particular, H-type groups constitute basic examples of H-type foliations; see \cite{Bau2022Htype}.

A useful feature of this model is that the canonical Bott, equivalently Hladky, connection associated with the splitting
\[
    TG=\mathcal H\oplus\mathcal V
\]
is flat. Indeed, with respect to any left-invariant adapted frame
\(\{e_i,e_\alpha\}\), the two-step nilpotent structure gives
\[
    \nabla_{e_A}e_B=0,
\]
and consequently
\[
    R^\nabla\equiv0,
    \qquad
    \ricci_{\mathcal H}^{\nabla}\equiv0.
\]
Notice, however,
that the sub-Riemannian geometry is still nontrivial, since
\[
    T(X,Y)=-[X,Y],
    \qquad X,Y\in\mathcal H,
\]
is generally nonzero. The H-type condition gives strong algebraic
control of this torsion through the maps \(J_Z\). Hence H-type groups
provide a large family of examples in which the adapted connection is
flat while the non-integrability of the horizontal distribution is
entirely encoded by the torsion.
